wiki-iran.standing: A count of how many people open the English Wikipedia article on Iran each day. It is a rough gauge of public attention to the country — the share of readers who go looking for background rather than headlines when Iran is in play.
wiki-iran.recent: Attention has fallen through a month of stalled Hormuz diplomacy. The 19 July peak came while the strait stayed shut; since then Iran has set six conditions and a reparations clause for reopening, Araghchi has denied any negotiation, and the story has narrowed to procedure — even the US firing on a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman drew fewer readers than July's fighting.

brent.standing: The price of a barrel of North Sea crude, and the benchmark most of the world's oil is priced against. It moves on supply — a strike, a sanction, a strait — and fuel, freight and fertiliser move after it.
brent.recent: The war premium has drained out since May's high of 116.70. Iran still keeps the Strait of Hormuz closed, with 8 to 15 ships crossing daily, but talks in Oman have made progress and Trump halted attacks on Iranian infrastructure on 2 August. Strikes on refineries in Zawiya, Jazan and Nizhnekamsk hit processing, not crude supply.

wti.standing: The US benchmark crude price, priced at a pipeline hub in Oklahoma and the reference most American oil is sold against. It moves on supply — a strike, a sanction, a strait — and fuel, freight and fertiliser move after it.
wti.recent: Crude has given back a fifth since peaking at $112.30 on May 18, as the Hormuz standoff eased on reopening hopes and futures fell again on Trump's 'good talks' comment on Iran. Drone strikes on Russian refineries and on Libya's Zawiya have kept it above the Jul 6 low of $69.60.

natgas-hh.standing: The US benchmark price for natural gas, quoted at a Louisiana pipeline junction and used to settle North American gas contracts. It sets what utilities, chemical plants and LNG exporters pay for fuel, and it swings hard on weather and storage.
natgas-hh.recent: Gas held near the bottom of its range through the summer, bottoming at $2.58 on Jul 29 before edging back to $2.81. Demand-side news has run ahead of the price: SpaceX is building its own gas power plants for a Texas chip factory and Amazon is funding a Fort Stockton plant of 35 turbines, both bypassing the grid for datacentre and fab loads.

wheat.standing: The world price of a tonne of wheat, the cereal that feeds more people directly than any other. It moves on harvests, export policy and the cost of fertiliser and fuel, and bread prices follow it into importing countries within months.
wheat.recent: Wheat has climbed off its September 2025 low of $155.1 to $199.6, peaking at $220.9 in May 2026, and the pass-through is visible downstream: the FAO's food price index hit 131.1, US diesel at $5.36 a gallon is lifting freight into every cereal chain, and a 20kg flour bag in Karachi now costs Rs3,000.

rice.standing: The world benchmark price for a tonne of milled rice, the staple calorie for more than half the planet. It moves on monsoon rainfall, export bans and stockpiling, and it passes almost directly into household food bills across Asia and West Africa.
rice.recent: Rice has fallen 29% over the series and sits near the October 2025 low of $330.6, well below its August 2024 high — a divergence from cereals generally, with the Food and Agriculture Organization's price index at 131.1 as heatwaves and wars push up crop costs. A second monsoon spell arriving on saturated ground in Pakistan puts a major exporter's crop at risk.

copper.standing: The price of a tonne of refined copper, the metal that carries electricity in every grid, motor, transformer and building. Demand for it tracks electrification and construction directly, which is why it is read as a gauge of industrial expansion.
copper.recent: Copper sits at its series high of $13,550/mt in June 2026, roughly half again above the $8,910 low of December 2024. The input does not name the supply or demand event behind the rise.

us-10y.standing: The yield on ten-year US government debt, the benchmark price of borrowing dollars for a decade. Mortgages, corporate loans and asset prices worldwide are priced off it, so a move here reprices almost everything else.
us-10y.recent: The Fed held rates at 350-375 basis points on 29 July, citing elevated, fuel-led inflation, and the yield peaked at 4.75% two days later. It has since eased to 4.65% as a further hike fell into doubt — the same repricing that dragged the dollar to its weakest since May on 7 August.

sp500.standing: The main US stock index, tracking 500 large American companies, and the benchmark most equity money in the world is measured against. It is the reference price for corporate profits and, through pension and index funds, for household wealth.
sp500.recent: The index sits near its high after the Fed held interest rates steady on 29 July, citing 'elevated' inflation. The move up came despite a repricing of AI spending: Alphabet's stock fell 7% on the same capex it used to cheer, and a fund built on AI conviction sold its AI position. Oil eased and stocks gained on Hormuz reopening hopes on 4 August.

nasdaq100.standing: A stock index tracking the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, weighted by market value. It is dominated by big technology firms, so it moves as a proxy for what investors will pay for computing, software and chips.
nasdaq100.recent: The index sits below its Jun 2 high of 30,660 after touching 27,190 on Jul 29, with the AI build-out reshaping the balance sheets underneath it: Nvidia arranged $500 billion in debt through six lenders to finance chip purchases, Meta gave away a 30-billion-parameter model that runs on a single consumer GPU, and DRAM jumped from $39 to $145.

us-gas-retail.standing: The average pump price for a gallon of regular gasoline across US filling stations, tracked weekly by the Energy Information Administration. It follows crude oil and refining margins with a lag, and it is the price most Americans feel first when energy markets move.
us-gas-retail.recent: Refineries have been the target rather than the oilfields: Ukrainian drones hit two Russian refineries on 6 August and reached Nizhnekamsk, 1,600 km from the border, on 10 August, while a third drone strike burned Libya's Zawiya refinery. Crude supply is untouched, so US pump prices have kept easing from their 18 May high of $4.49.

natgas-ttf.standing: The European benchmark price for wholesale natural gas, set at a Dutch virtual trading hub. It is what the continent's power stations, heating and heavy industry pay for gas, and it moves on pipeline and LNG supply.
natgas-ttf.recent: Supply infrastructure has been the pressure point. A drone strike on floating storage at Egypt's Damietta LNG terminal on 29 July set fire to one tanker and then a second, and the Nord Stream sabotage remains unresolved, with Russia pressing Germany to identify those behind the blasts.

vix.standing: A CBOE index of expected S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days, derived from options prices. It rises when traders pay up for protection, which is why it is read as a gauge of how much stress the equity market is pricing.
vix.recent: Volatility priced out of markets as global equities hit record highs through early August, with the index settling near its low. The same calm reached crypto: traders described the bitcoin sell-off from $65,000 as thin volume rather than panic, and bitcoin ETFs took in $754 million on 7 August as options skew flattened.

fx-pkr.standing: The exchange rate of Pakistan's currency against the US dollar, quoted as rupees per dollar. Pakistan imports most of its fuel and much of its food, so the rate sets the domestic price of both and shapes the cost of servicing external debt.
fx-pkr.recent: The rupee has been steady near 277.5 through a month of domestic strain: Jamaat-e-Islami counted 510 protests in a single day over the petroleum levy, goods transporters kept striking as diesel prices changed daily, and the Karachi benchmark index fell for a second day on the Hormuz standoff. The finance ministry has forecast inflation of 9-10%.

fx-ngn.standing: The exchange rate of Nigeria's currency against the US dollar. Nigeria imports most of its refined fuel, wheat and medicine, so the naira rate sets domestic prices, and oil sales supply the dollars that back it.
fx-ngn.recent: The naira held in a narrow band through a month of domestic political strain rather than economic shock: a coup-financing trail in which a currency dealer moved 785 million naira to plotters, Tinubu's order overriding the EFCC freeze on Osun state accounts, and an aviation union strike that grounded flights in Lagos.

fx-egp.standing: Egypt's currency measured against the dollar. The country imports most of its wheat and fuel and owes large debts in dollars, so this rate sets the domestic price of bread, medicine and almost everything shipped in.
fx-egp.recent: The pound has been close to flat over the month, weakest at 51.37 on Jul 25 and strongest at 49.56 on Aug 8. What the rate has already done is visible at the counter in Cairo, where a price freeze held against an earlier devaluation has turned a drug shortage into an empty shelf.

fx-try.standing: The exchange rate of Turkey's currency against the dollar. A managed float that has slid for years under high inflation, it sets the price of everything Turkey imports — energy, grain, machinery — and the cost of its dollar debt.
fx-try.recent: The lira drifted to a 30-day low of 47.77 on Aug 12 through a month of Turkish diplomatic and security news rather than any monetary event: the Mecca joint defence pact signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on Aug 7, a Kurdish disarmament law passed Aug 10, and drone strikes on Turkish shipping near Novorossiysk.

fx-bdt.standing: The Bangladeshi taka's price against the US dollar. A managed float in a country whose economy runs on garment exports and worker remittances in dollars, and which pays for fuel, food grain and industrial inputs in the same currency.
fx-bdt.recent: The taka firmed slightly over the month, easing from 124 on Aug 7 to 123.4. Nothing in the record explains the move: the period's Bangladesh news was diplomatic rather than economic, centred on Dhaka pressing Delhi over ex-PM Hasina's planned virtual address, which India denied involvement in.

fx-idr.standing: Indonesia's currency, quoted as rupiah per US dollar, so a rising number means a weaker rupiah. It is among the emerging-market currencies most sensitive to US interest rates and to commodity prices, since Indonesia funds a large budget partly through foreign holdings of its bonds.
fx-idr.recent: The rupiah firmed through the window, from 18,110 on Jul 28 to 17,800 on Aug 8, and rose again on Aug 11 when Prabowo nominated Bank Indonesia's deputy governor Destry Damayanti to run the central bank. The market is pricing one question: whether an internal career official will finance the president's spending, as BI did during the pandemic.

fx-lbp.standing: The Lebanese pound's exchange rate against the US dollar, fixed by the central bank since the 2019 banking collapse wiped out most of its value. Lebanese salaries, savings and import prices are all read through it.
fx-lbp.recent: The pound barely moved across the month, holding near its peg through a period in which the fighting did not pause: Israeli strikes and demolitions hit towns across the south, one levelling two apartment blocks in Beirut, while a seventh round of direct talks in Rome stalled. Lebanese officials count 4,333 killed in the south since March.

fx-cny.standing: China's currency, quoted as yuan per US dollar, and the price at which the world's largest exporter's goods are converted into everyone else's money. Beijing manages it within a band, so a move is as much a policy signal as a market one.
fx-cny.recent: The yuan drifted stronger across the window, from 6.782 on Jul 14 to 6.745 on Aug 11, a move of about half a percent — narrow enough to sit inside ordinary managed-float trading. Nothing in the period's China news, from Typhoon Dolphin's landfall and the pre-emptive port closures to Beijing's tightened drone export rules, marks a distinct turn in the series.

fx-inr.standing: The rupee's exchange rate against the dollar, the price at which India settles its imported oil, fertiliser and electronics. India runs a persistent trade deficit, so a weaker rupee raises the domestic cost of nearly everything the country buys abroad.
fx-inr.recent: The rupee has held in a narrow band, strengthening from 96.65 on Jul 18 to 95.05 by Aug 5 before easing to 95.42. Nothing in the window explains a move that small: the oil price fell 4.5% in early August on a remark about Iran, which cuts India's largest import bill, and Tata Sons faces a chairman's possible exit before an August 18 vote.

fx-brl.standing: The exchange rate between Brazil's real and the US dollar, the price at which the largest economy in Latin America trades with the world. It moves on domestic politics and on US interest rates, and it sets the cost of Brazil's imports and the dollar value of its soy, beef and iron exports.
fx-brl.recent: The real drifted to its weakest level of the month against the dollar as a diplomatic rupture with Washington deepened: the US revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador on 4 August, saying it would restore it only if Brasília accepted its own envoy pick. Two days earlier, Lula was nominated for a fourth term.

fx-mxn.standing: The exchange rate between Mexico's peso and the US dollar, one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies. Mexico sends most of its exports north, so the rate carries US demand, trade policy and interest-rate decisions straight into Mexican prices and wages.
fx-mxn.recent: The peso strengthened through the window, from 17.54 on Jul 19 to 17.06 on Aug 12. The month's Mexico news ran to security and disease rather than the economy: a $25 million US bounty on a cartel leader in Guadalajara, the Sinaloa Cartel splitting into rival factions, and screwworm cases passing 500.

fx-eur.standing: The exchange rate between the euro and the US dollar, quoted here as euros per dollar. It is the most traded currency pair in the world, and it sets the import cost of energy and dollar-priced commodities for the twenty countries that use the euro.
fx-eur.recent: The euro drifted lower across the month, from 0.8792 per dollar on 26 July to 0.8651 on 8 August before steadying at 0.8669. Nothing in the reporting from this window explains the move.

fx-jpy.standing: Japan's currency, and the funding leg of the world's largest carry trade: decades of near-zero rates made borrowing yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad routine, so its swings propagate into markets that have nothing to do with Japan.
fx-jpy.recent: Tokyo sold dollars for yen hours before the Bank of Japan held rates at 1% on 31 July, and the yen surged on the suspected intervention; the US then joined a historic joint intervention on 3 August, pushing the dollar to a one-month low. The cheap yen has flattered exporters — Toyota's quarterly profit nearly doubled to $9.4 billion.

fx-rub.standing: The exchange rate between Russia's ruble and the US dollar, quoted as rubles per dollar, so a rising number means a weaker ruble. It is the cleanest daily read on how sanctions, oil receipts and capital controls are landing on the Russian economy.
fx-rub.recent: The ruble has weakened through a month of escalation: Ukrainian drones reached 1,600 km inside Russia at Nizhnekamsk, killing 13 and hitting a refinery, while a sanctioned tanker leaked off Oman and Moscow's Deputy Foreign Minister Galuzin ruled out a freeze in Ukraine. It hit 83 to the dollar on Aug 7.

fx-zar.standing: The exchange rate of South Africa's currency against the US dollar, one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies. It swings on commodity prices, global risk appetite and domestic politics, and it sets the cost of imported fuel and food.
fx-zar.recent: The rand firmed to 16.19 from a 16.83 peak on Jul 25, touching 16.15 on Aug 8. Little in the domestic record explains the move: the month's news was municipal electricity surcharges of up to 14% in Johannesburg and a Prasa security-contract investigation in Pretoria, neither of which is a currency driver.

btc.standing: The first cryptocurrency and the largest by market value, traded around the clock against dollars. It has no issuer and no yield, so its price is set purely by what buyers will pay, which makes it move on liquidity, regulation and confidence in custody.
btc.recent: Custody failures have set the tone: a Coldcard hack drained $120 million and the attacker's own transactions congested the network, while attackers separately drained Foundation's and Citadel21's Lightning nodes. Bitcoin fell 4% against every other market signal and now sits 49% below its record, even as ETFs took in $754 million and volatility nearly vanished.

eth.standing: The second-largest cryptocurrency by value, and the settlement layer most stablecoins, tokenised assets and decentralised exchanges are built on. Its price moves with crypto risk appetite and with rules written for the dollar tokens riding on it.
eth.recent: The move came against a tightening regulatory frame rather than any single shock: the Senate's Clarity Act missed its pre-recess vote window, Treasury sanctioned an Iranian dollar-token exchange rather than a bank, Brazil imposed a 24-hour delay on crypto transfers above $10,000, and South Korea set a 2027 tax on gains over $1,740.

paxg.standing: A token backed one-for-one by allocated gold bullion, tracking the spot price of an ounce. It is where money goes when currencies, sovereign debt or the banking system look less safe, and it pays nothing while it waits.
paxg.recent: Gold rose to $4,390 an ounce on Aug 11, up roughly a tenth over the month from $3,982 on Jul 17. The input does not explain what drove the move.

wiki-artificial-intelligence.standing: A field of computer science building systems that perform tasks once requiring human judgement — recognition, language, prediction. Its Wikipedia article is the general-audience entry point, so readership rises when the technology reaches people outside the industry.
wiki-artificial-intelligence.recent: The week's readership followed AI leaving the lab: a Stanford model designed 16 working virus genomes, reported across 319 outlets, and Zuckerberg published a 6,500-word manifesto on superintelligence. Nvidia arranged $500 billion in lending to finance its own chips, and Pakistan made an AI course mandatory for every degree.

wiki-russia.standing: Wikipedia's Russia article, and how many people open it each day. Attention to a country page is a rough gauge of how far a war or a crisis has spread beyond the people already following it.
wiki-russia.recent: The peak on Aug 8 sat between two rounds of strikes reaching far inside Russia: drones hit Nizhnekamsk, 1,600 km from the Ukrainian border, killing 13 including a child, and Kamchatka's ballistic-missile submarines were put under rope netting at the pier. Moscow then ruled out a freeze in Ukraine, with Deputy Foreign Minister Galuzin rejecting the terms.

wiki-pakistan.standing: Daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on Pakistan, a country of some 250 million people with nuclear weapons, a powerful army and long borders with India, Iran, China and Afghanistan. Attention to it tends to follow security shocks.
wiki-pakistan.recent: The late-July peak came as reports circulated that Iran would receive Chinese missiles and air defences despite Xi's pledge to Trump, before a suicide attack on a protest in Pakistan's Swat district on 2 August. Readership held up through the Mecca defence pact signed 7 August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.

wiki-china.standing: The pageview count for Wikipedia's article on China, a rough daily gauge of how many people worldwide go looking for background on the country. It rises when China does something that sends readers to check the basics.
wiki-china.recent: The 10 August peak followed Typhoon Dolphin's landfall, before which China evacuated over a million people and closed major ports a full day early. Beijing also deleted AI companion chatbots, codified Xinjiang's campaign-era restrictions into national law, and issued a climate-only five-year plan.

wiki-strait-of-hormuz.standing: The 33-kilometre-wide sea lane between Iran and Oman that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil out of the Gulf. It has no bypass at scale, so any interruption to it is priced into crude, freight and war-risk insurance worldwide.
wiki-strait-of-hormuz.recent: Views peaked on 14 Jul and have fallen by two thirds since, tracking the closure's slide from crisis to negotiation. Trump halted a planned attack on Iran on 2 Aug and then claimed the US fully controls the strait; Oman and Qatar brokered progress, and Iran attached six conditions plus a reparations clause to reopening. Transits are down a third, at 8 to 15 ships a day.

wiki-bitcoin.standing: A daily count of how many people open Wikipedia's Bitcoin article — a rough gauge of public curiosity about the cryptocurrency, which rises when a hack, a price break or a governance fight pushes it past the people who already follow it.
wiki-bitcoin.recent: Readership tracked a run of failures rather than a price move: the Coldcard hack drained $120 million and the attacker's own transactions congested Bitcoin, one firmware bug cost $88 million, and attackers drained Foundation's and Citadel21's Lightning nodes. Bitcoin sits 49% below its record.

wiki-saudi-arabia.standing: Wikipedia's article on Saudi Arabia, and the count of how many people read it each day. Attention tracks the kingdom's role as the world's swing oil producer and the custodian of Islam's two holiest cities, so it rises whenever either is in play.
wiki-saudi-arabia.recent: Saudi Arabia entered the U.S.-Iran war with strikes in Iraq in late July, then signed a joint defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan in Mecca on 7 August — an agreement Egypt declined to join and one that never states whose nuclear deterrent applies. Houthi missiles hit Najran the same week, wounding 11.

wiki-donald-trump.standing: Daily readership of the Wikipedia biography of the sitting US president. It is a gauge of how many people are looking him up rather than of what they think, and it has a high floor that any decision, ruling or foreign trip lifts sharply.
wiki-donald-trump.recent: The strongest pull was the Strait of Hormuz: Trump halted the attack on Iran on 2 August, then claimed the US fully controls the strait, while talks with Iran and Oman moved toward a transit deal. The most recent climb followed his 11 August departure from Ankara hidden inside a catering truck under an Iranian threat.

wiki-india.standing: One of the most-read country articles on Wikipedia, tracking daily readership of the encyclopedia's overview of India. Attention to it rises and falls with what the country's 1.4 billion people are doing in the world's news.
wiki-india.recent: On 4 August India added heatwaves and lightning to its schedule of notified natural disasters, letting states draw on national disaster funds for heat relief for the first time. A US Senate bill threatening 100% tariffs on India put the country's strategic autonomy in question, and Modi inaugurated the Param Pragya AI supercomputer at Sonipat.

wiki-israel.standing: The Wikipedia article on Israel, and how many people open it each day. Attention to a country page is a rough proxy for how far a story about it has travelled beyond the people already following it.
wiki-israel.recent: Readership rose through a week of Israeli operations across three fronts: more than 500 attacks recorded in the West Bank, demolitions and drone bombs in south Lebanon towns including Mansouri, and Netanyahu's rejection of the Gaza roadmap on an election calendar set by an October 27 vote. Venezuela also restored consular ties severed for 17 years.

wiki-united-states.standing: The Wikipedia article on the United States, one of the most-read country pages on the site. Daily readership rises when the country is at the centre of a war, an election or a court fight, so the curve is a rough gauge of how much of the world is looking at Washington at once.
wiki-united-states.recent: Readership sat near its high through the Strait of Hormuz standoff, when Trump halted attacks on Iran's infrastructures and then claimed the US fully controls the strait. It has drifted down since as talks with Iran to reopen the strait made progress, with US diesel at $5.36 a gallon the residue at home.

wiki-ukraine.standing: A count of how many people read the English Wikipedia article on Ukraine each day. It is a measure of public attention rather than of events, and it rises when something happens that sends people looking for background.
wiki-ukraine.recent: The series drifted down through late July and hit its 30-day low of 7,255 on 8 Aug, then turned back up as the war reached deeper targets: a Ukrainian drone strike on Nizhnekamsk, 1,600 km from the border, killed 13 including a child on 10 Aug, and Russian missiles hit a children's hospital in Kyiv.

wiki-nigeria.standing: Wikipedia's page for Nigeria, and how many people open it each day. Africa's most populous country and its largest oil producer, so attention here tends to rise with elections, security crises and anything that moves the naira.
wiki-nigeria.recent: The peak on Jul 27 came amid the Osun contest, where police were booed as APC and Accord supporters clashed at a stakeholders' forum, a dispute that reached Tinubu ordering the EFCC to vacate its freeze on the Osun account. Readership has fallen by roughly a third since.

cp:hormuz.standing: One-fifth of global seaborne oil passes through this 21-mile strait between Iran and Oman.
cp:hormuz.recent: Iran keeps the strait closed, setting six conditions for reopening and adding a reparations clause as the 60-day deal window narrowed to a week; 8 to 15 ships now cross daily. US forces fired two Hellfire missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman for running the blockade. Crude from Iraq now moves overland through Syria instead.

cp:bab-el-mandeb.standing: Between Yemen and Djibouti — the Red Sea’s southern gate. Houthi attacks since 2023 have pushed container shipping to reroute around Africa.
cp:bab-el-mandeb.recent: Traffic has fallen as Houthi strikes reached the strait itself: six sailors died in a Bab al-Mandeb strike reported on 11 August, an Indian-flagged vessel was sunk off Mokha on 4 August, and missiles hit the Mokha coast and the Jazan refinery on 9 August. Crossings dropped to 18 ships on 3 August from 28 two days earlier, and escort requests are up 39% since February.

cp:suez.standing: Egypt’s 120-mile artery carries roughly 12% of global trade. The 2021 closure disrupted supply chains for weeks; Red Sea instability keeps it volatile.
cp:suez.recent: Transits are running at roughly half their 90-day baseline as attacks continue at the canal's southern approach: six sailors died in a Bab al-Mandeb strike on a cargo ship, and a projectile sank the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya off Mokha on 4 August. Houthi strikes also hit Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery and Egypt's Damietta gas port.

cp:malacca.standing: Between Malaysia and Sumatra — the fastest route between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Over 80,000 ships a year, including most of China’s oil imports.
cp:malacca.recent: Transits have fallen from 263 vessels a day on Jun 22 to 207, with the low of 170 on Jul 19. The Hormuz closure is the visible pressure: Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia has dropped, and Hormuz vessel transits have fallen to a fraction, cutting the westbound tanker flow that feeds the strait.

cp:taiwan.standing: Between mainland China and Taiwan — roughly 40% of the world’s container traffic passes through, and the flashpoint of any US–China confrontation.
cp:taiwan.recent: Typhoon Dolphin drove the swing: China closed major ports a full day before landfall and evacuated over a million people, and vessel counts collapsed to 28 on Jul 10 before rebounding to 401 on Jul 12 as backlogged ships sailed. Traffic is now running 15.2% below its 90-day baseline.

cp:panama.standing: 50-mile shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. Drought in 2023–24 cut daily transits by half — a live example of climate binding to trade.
cp:panama.recent: Transits stand at 29 vessels a day, down 12% across the window and about 5% below the 90-day baseline, after a swing from 83 on Jul 13 to 22 on Jul 22. The coverage does not explain that swing.

cp:bosporus.standing: Istanbul’s 20-mile waterway links the Black Sea to the Mediterranean — the only route for Russian naval access and Ukrainian grain exports.
cp:bosporus.recent: Traffic is down about a fifth against its own 90-day baseline as the war reached the shipping itself: drones struck the Turkish-operated Nadezhda near Novorossiysk, sank a Rosatom freighter at the same port, and killed a crewman on a coal-hauling tanker. Turkey has since turned back some vessels bound for Novorossiysk.

cp:gibraltar.standing: 8 miles between Morocco and Spain — the only Atlantic–Mediterranean link. A surveillance chokepoint for Russian submarines and sanctioned oil.
cp:gibraltar.recent: Daily transits have eased from a peak of 163 on Jun 13 to 112, but the past week sits level with the strait's own 90-day baseline, and seas topped out at 0.6 m. The record shows no closure, weather event or rerouting behind the decline — this is ordinary summer variation, not a disruption.

cp:dover.standing: The busiest shipping lane on Earth — 400+ ships a day squeeze through the English Channel’s 21-mile narrows.
cp:dover.recent: Traffic has run close to its 90-day baseline, and the low of 126 on Aug 3 sits alongside a summer of heat in the Channel rather than any closure: Western Europe recorded its hottest June and July on record, and jellyfish drawn to warm water shut three reactors at Gravelines on the French coast. A migrant dinghy carrying about 160 people caught fire mid-Channel on Aug 4.

cp:cape-of-good-hope.standing: The 3,000-mile detour around southern Africa — the alternative when the Red Sea is closed. The new default for tankers since Houthi attacks began.
cp:cape-of-good-hope.recent: Traffic has fallen about 30% over the window, from 161 vessels a day in mid-May to 83, with the low of 68 on Jul 4. The input does not explain the decline. Very rough seas, with waves to 4.1m, cover the latest readings.

cp:kerch.standing: Between Crimea and Russia — the only access to the Sea of Azov. A flashpoint since 2014 and contested throughout the Russia–Ukraine war.
cp:kerch.recent: Traffic has fallen to zero, down from 50 vessels a day in mid-May, with the last seven days running 98% below baseline. The collapse tracks the wider closure of Black Sea shipping: strikes have shut Odessa's ports and war-risk premiums now price ships out of calling there, and a drone killed one crewman on a Turkish coal-hauling tanker.

mkt:tadawul.standing: The Arab world’s largest exchange by market value, dominated by Aramco. Trades Sunday to Thursday, so it opens the global week before Tokyo.
mkt:tadawul.recent: Saudi Arabia has been drawn into the region's war on both ends: it joined US strikes in Iraq in late July, and Houthi missiles have since hit Najran, Marib and the Jazan refinery that processes 400,000 barrels of crude daily. The index has drifted down through that, even as war-driven oil lifted Aramco profit 33%.

mkt:bist.standing: Türkiye’s only exchange. Priced in lira, so its index level carries the country’s inflation as much as its earnings — read the direction, not the number.
mkt:bist.recent: The index has fallen through a summer of security shocks around Turkey's coasts and borders: drones struck the Turkish-operated Nadezhda near Novorossiysk on 4 August, Ankara began rationing Bosphorus passage for some Novorossiysk-bound vessels, and Turkey signed a joint defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in Mecca on 7 August.

mkt:dfm.standing: The Gulf’s main listing venue for property and banking. Moved from a Sunday–Thursday week to Monday–Friday in 2022, unlike Riyadh.
mkt:dfm.recent: The index sits near the middle of its range after a run of shocks to Dubai's standing as a trade and finance hub: seven blasts in twenty minutes hit Jebel Ali port on 5 August, and Iran's demand for an Iranian-controlled inbound lane through Hormuz put the emirate's main shipping approach in question. The 18 June high has not been retested.

mkt:bursa-malaysia.standing: The world’s largest market for Islamic finance instruments, and the centre of the global sukuk trade.
mkt:bursa-malaysia.recent: The index has drifted lower as the Hormuz closure worked its way into Malaysian refineries: Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia has dropped, with vessel transits through the strait falling to a fraction of normal. Politics compounded it — Anwar Ibrahim's coalition lost Negeri Sembilan to a Malay-nationalist wave on 3 August, and the DAP scheduled a vote on staying in the unity government.

mkt:idx.standing: The exchange of the world’s largest Muslim-majority country, heavily weighted to commodities and banking.
mkt:idx.recent: The index sits about 8% below where it was two months ago, and has recovered from a low on Jun 8 to 6310. Prabowo has nominated Bank Indonesia's deputy governor Destry Damayanti as governor, and the rupiah rose slightly on the news — a currency call on whether the new governor will finance the president's spending, which the equity market reads the same way.

mkt:tse.standing: Asia’s largest exchange, and the first major market to price each trading day.
mkt:tse.recent: The index has been driven by the yen. The Bank of Japan held rates at 1% on 31 July, and Toyota's quarterly profit nearly doubled to $9.4 billion on the cheap yen; the joint US-Japan intervention announced 3 August pushed the dollar to a one-month low, taking that support away.

mkt:hkex.standing: Where mainland Chinese companies meet foreign capital — the clearest daily read on sentiment toward China.
mkt:hkex.recent: The index has drifted lower across the window, down 3.8% from its 14 May high of 26,390 and 1.2% on the day. Beijing tightened drone exports into a fresh trade clash with Washington, ordered chatbot companion services deleted, and Typhoon Dolphin forced port closures and the evacuation of over a million people before landfall.

mkt:sse.standing: Mainland China’s main board. Largely closed to foreign investors, so it tracks domestic policy more than global risk appetite.
mkt:sse.recent: The index sits roughly 6% below its May 13 high of 4,243, with an ongoing floor at 3,764 on July 17. Beijing tightened drone exports in a fresh trade clash with Washington, Trump set a polysilicon price floor aimed at Chinese solar supply, and Typhoon Dolphin forced port closures and the evacuation of over a million people.

mkt:krx.standing: Dominated by Samsung and SK Hynix — a proxy for the global semiconductor cycle.
mkt:krx.recent: The index is riding the memory cycle in both directions. It set its largest single-day gain ever on 31 July after its steepest three-day rout, as Samsung reported profit up 1,814% on AI chip demand and warned of shortage through 2028; SK Hynix then dropped 5% on a $38B fab bet, with all 2027 capacity already sold out.

mkt:bse.standing: Asia’s oldest exchange, founded 1875, and the benchmark for Indian equities.
mkt:bse.recent: The index sits near the top of its 65-day range after climbing from a June 8 low, but the coverage does not explain the move. The one Mumbai corporate story in view is Tata Sons: chairman Chandrasekaran may quit before an August 18 vote tied to an RBI listing requirement.

mkt:sgx.standing: Southeast Asia’s financial hub, weighted to banks and regional property.
mkt:sgx.recent: The index closed at 5732, a fraction below the 5754 high it set on 11 August and up roughly 16 percent from its 12 May low of 4946. Nothing in the available material accounts for the climb.

mkt:twse.standing: TSMC alone is roughly a third of the index, which makes this the most concentrated major market on the map.
mkt:twse.recent: The index has recovered from its 30 July low, though the ground under it is uneven: chipmaking employs few of Taiwan's workers, leaving a two-speed economy where the boom is concentrated in fabs. Two Chinese coast guard ships drifted off Orchid Island, east of Taiwan, on 31 July, near the series trough.

mkt:set.standing: Thailand’s benchmark, sensitive to tourism flows and regional energy prices.
mkt:set.recent: The index has recovered from its May low but slipped on the day, with Bangkok absorbing two political shocks in one week: the visit of Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2021 coup, and a school shooting in Nonthaburi that killed eight and wounded 15, after which the Thai PM vowed stricter gun laws.

mkt:pse.standing: A small, domestically-driven market where remittance flows move the index.
mkt:pse.recent: The index sits near the top of its 48-day range after climbing from the May 29 low of 5,769, but slipped 1.2% as the Sara Duterte impeachment trial reached Day 14 with confidential fund disbursements recorded to names like Miggy Mango and Jay Kamote against zero results. Manila's South China Sea posture and a magnitude 6.3 earthquake in the southern Philippines fell inside the same window.

mkt:asx.standing: Mining and banking. Often the first major market to react to Chinese demand data.
mkt:asx.recent: The RBA held its cash rate steady on 11 August as the housing market softened, leaving the index near the 9,272 peak it set on 6 August. The heavier drag is structural: China's steel stock has aged enough to recycle, and a shift toward scrap skips the iron ore that underwrites much of the index's resource earnings.

mkt:jse.standing: Africa’s largest exchange by far, and the continent’s only one with a usable public daily series.
mkt:jse.recent: The index fell to 108,300 on Jul 23 before recovering most of the loss, and is down slightly over the window. Domestic cost pressure runs through the same consumer names that anchor the index: electricity bills rose up to 14% this month after municipal surcharge increases, pushing households toward cheaper food baskets.

mkt:b3.standing: Latin America’s largest exchange, driven by iron ore, oil and Brazilian rates.
mkt:b3.recent: The index closed at its 66-day low on Aug 11, down 7.7% from its May 11 high, with a 2.5% fall on the day. Brazilian politics turned in the same window: Washington revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador and said it would restore it only if Brasília accepts its own envoy pick, and Lula was nominated for a fourth term at 81.

mkt:bmv.standing: Mexico’s benchmark, tightly coupled to US demand and the peso.
mkt:bmv.recent: The index has fallen through a summer of compounding trouble in Mexico: a screwworm parasite eradicated in 2003 has returned with human cases past 500, and the US put a $25 million bounty on a top Mexican drug cartel leader. The low came on Jun 10 at 64,820; the drop since May 11 is roughly 7%.

mkt:byma.standing: Priced in a currency that has lost most of its value repeatedly, so the index rises even in bad years. Direction over a day means something; the level does not.

mkt:tsx.standing: Energy, mining and banks — a commodity index wearing an equity index’s clothes.
mkt:tsx.recent: The index reached 36,480 on Aug 11, the high of a 64-day run up 6.8% from its May 19 low of 33,740. The input does not identify what drove the advance.

mkt:nyse.standing: The largest equity market on earth. Its close sets the tone every other market opens against.
mkt:nyse.recent: The index sits near its 63-day high after a run through a fortnight of Gulf escalation: US missiles hit a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman for trying to break the Iran blockade, while talks with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz made progress and Trump halted planned attacks on Iranian infrastructure. Diesel at $5.36 a gallon carries the war premium into food prices.

mkt:lse.standing: Most FTSE 100 revenue is earned abroad, so a falling pound tends to push the index up.
mkt:lse.recent: The index sits at 10840, near its Jul 29 high of 10910 and up about 5.6% over the series, with little in the record to explain the drift; the day's move was a 0.17% slip. Nothing in London's news window — a prison-release fight over PC Harper's killers, a ban on fake discounts — bears on it.

mkt:xetra.standing: Germany’s industrial and chemical base — Europe’s clearest export barometer.
mkt:xetra.recent: The index reached 26390 on Aug 11, the top of its 67-day range, even as German industry shed staff: BMW is cutting 8,000 jobs worldwide and Porsche another 5,000. Commerzbank has warmed to a UniCredit takeover Berlin once called a sovereignty threat, and Adidas reported strong growth on the World Cup.

mkt:euronext-paris.standing: Luxury goods and energy dominate — unusually exposed to Chinese consumer demand.
mkt:euronext-paris.recent: The index set its 67-day high on Aug 10 and has drifted since, closing at 8715. Nothing in the week's French news bears directly on the move: the reactor outages at Gravelines, where jellyfish knocked out 3.2 gigawatts of nuclear power, and the record European heat left the index broadly flat.

mkt:euronext-amsterdam.standing: The world’s oldest exchange, now carried largely by ASML.
mkt:euronext-amsterdam.recent: The index closed at a 67-day high on Aug 11, up about 10% since its May 12 low, and the day's move was slight. Nothing in the record explains the climb.

mkt:bme.standing: Spanish banks with heavy Latin American exposure make this a proxy for both regions.
mkt:bme.recent: The index closed at 20,210 on 11 August, its high over the past 67 days and a 13.2% rise from the 12 May low of 17,570. The coverage available does not explain the move: Spain's news this period was dominated by the Ceuta crossings, reciprocal border checks with Italy, and the 12 August eclipse.

mkt:borsa-italiana.standing: Banks and utilities, and the market most sensitive to Italian sovereign debt spreads.
mkt:borsa-italiana.recent: The index closed at its 67-day high on 7 August, up about 9 percent over the window, as Italy's border dispute with Spain escalated without touching trade. Rome had suspended Schengen against Spain on 31 July after 72,000 people rushed the Ceuta enclave, and Madrid imposed reciprocal checks on 7 August. Milan-based Bending Spoons bought Airtable for $1.28bn on 4 August.

mkt:six.standing: Nestlé, Roche and Novartis carry the index, which makes it defensive when the world turns risk-off.

mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.standing: Nordic industrials and telecoms, and a useful early read on European capital spending.
mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.recent: The index sits near the top of its 65-day range after climbing from a 15 May low of 3036 to a 5 August high of 3327, easing 0.3% on the day. The coverage in this window points at Volkswagen, where the controlling families broke board silence to press management over excess capacity — a signal to the European industrial complex Stockholm's exporters sit inside.

mkt:tase.standing: Trades Sunday to Thursday. Heavily weighted to banks, defence and technology.
mkt:tase.recent: The index has fallen about 9.5% over the past three months, from a high of 4,463 on May 11 to 4,039, with a low of 3,966 on Jun 29. The available material does not explain the decline.

poly-israel-x-iran-ceasefire-continues-t.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether Israel and Iran reach a ceasefire by a set date, priced in percent. It pays out on the outcome, so the level is what traders will pay for a truce happening — not a forecast, and it moves with every step toward or away from one.
poly-israel-x-iran-ceasefire-continues-t.recent: Pricing collapsed the war's odds of continuing after Trump halted attacks on Iran's infrastructure on 2 August and talks with Iran, Oman and the US on reopening the Strait of Hormuz made progress. Iran has since reopened its damaged airports, though the Hormuz reopening remains conditional and US forces fired on a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman.

xag.standing: A silver price taken from Kinesis KAG, a token backed one-for-one by vaulted silver. Silver is both a monetary metal and an industrial input — solar cells, electronics, brazing — so it moves on investor demand and factory demand at once.
xag.recent: The price swung from $29.80 on Aug 6 to $63.25 on Aug 8 and has since settled at $61.73, leaving it higher across the month. What moved it is not in the record.

wiki-spain.standing: How many people read the English Wikipedia article on Spain each day. A country page's readership is a rough gauge of how far a story about that country has travelled beyond the people it directly affects.
wiki-spain.recent: Attention has fallen back by about a third since 20 July, when the Ceuta crossings peaked: nearly 60,000 people swam around the border fence of the Spanish enclave in a week, 57 bodies were recovered, and Italy reimposed border checks against Spain under Schengen. Spain answered with checks of its own on 7 August.

poly-will-the-fed-increase-interest-rate.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the Federal Reserve raises its policy rate at the September 2026 meeting. The price is what traders will pay for that outcome, so it moves with every signal about inflation, employment and the Fed's own guidance.
poly-will-the-fed-increase-interest-rate.recent: The Fed held rates at 350-375 basis points on 29 July while citing 'elevated' inflation, and analysts read the hold as hawkish; Citadel had bet on a hike. Pricing peaked at 60 on Aug 1 as oil surged back above $90 and the Fed signalled rates could still rise, then fell back to 39.

poly-will-the-us-invade-iran-before-2027.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the United States invades Iran before 2027, priced in cents on the dollar. It is what traders are willing to pay for that outcome, not a forecast, and it reprices fastest when the two governments talk or shoot.
poly-will-the-us-invade-iran-before-2027.recent: The price fell through late July and early August as Trump halted a planned attack on Iran's infrastructures and Oman-mediated talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz made progress, bottoming at 16 on Aug 6. It has since edged back to 19 after US forces fired two Hellfire missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman and reports of an Iranian threat that forced Trump into a secret flight from Ankara.

stocks:META.standing: Meta Platforms is the parent of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, and one of the largest advertising businesses on earth. Its share price is a proxy for how much investors will pay for attention — and, lately, for what that attention is spent building.
stocks:META.recent: The slide followed Meta's cash flow craters report on 30 July: free cash flow fell $8.55bn to $784 million in a year as Zuckerberg doubled down on AI spending. His 6,500-word manifesto on 10 August read as a capex document, and Meta gave away Glimmer, a 30-billion-parameter model, the same day. A New Mexico judge also ordered $567 million in a kids online safety case.
